title: Corrupted (Sn 4.3)
hookLine: read it: people who praise their own view
tomorrow: if not by being right, how does anyone become pure?

cards: The humblebrag has a recognizable shape. So tired after volunteering all weekend. Can't believe I got picked again.
Ugh, being the reliable one is exhausting. Nobody asked, and the praise arrives anyway, dressed as a complaint. The third poem in the chapter of eights has a word for this, and it isn't a gentle one.
It also has a reason, which turns out to matter more than the scolding.

teach.b: Here's the question the poem asks: why does praising your own view, or your own goodness, go wrong? In paraphrase: some speak from a corrupted mind, some from a true one, and the sage stays out of the quarrel either way.
How would anyone get past their own view, led by what they like, settled in what they prefer? They make it complete for themselves and speak from there.

teach.h: UNASKED, THE SKILLED CALL IT IGNOBLE.
teach.b: Then the line: whoever praises their own virtue and practices to others, without being asked, the skilled call that ignoble. The one at peace, who doesn't boast I am like this, they call noble. So that's the answer.

teach.h: A VIEW ADVERTISED IS A VIEW DEFENDED.
teach.b: Praising your view isn't only bad manners. It digs you in. Once a view is something you advertise, it's something you have to defend, and the quarrel is already on its way.
A neighbor tradition says something close.

In Proverbs, a book Jews and Christians both keep, the King James Version reads: "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips." Shared: don't be your own fan club.
Proverbs moves the praise; let someone else give it, and it can be good. The poem goes further. Its sage has let go of holding views as a self to defend, and so has nothing to advertise at all.

how: Monastic codes in Buddhist traditions discourage monks and nuns from boasting about their attainments, and teachers point students to poems like this one on clinging to views; Proverbs is read in Jewish and Christian study and worship.

o: stolen or copied from somebody else's work
spoiled by self-praise and a dug-in view
forgotten over time, like a fading memory

games.q: the poem and its neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: the boast the one at peace won't make

s: Buddhism says having opinions at all is wrong
the poem's trouble is praising your own view and virtue unasked, and getting dug in to defend it.
the poem calls praising your own virtue, unasked, ignoble
and calls the one at peace, who won't boast 'I am like this', noble.
Proverbs and this poem say exactly the same thing
both warn against self-praise. Proverbs lets another give praise; the poem's sage has no self-view to advertise.

games.q: you spent your Saturday at a food bank and want people to know. by the poem, what's the move?
o: let the deed stand; it doesn't need your praise on top.
post it, since it might inspire others to volunteer.
stop volunteering, since you'll only end up bragging.
games.why: the poem doesn't fault the deed, only the praise you add to it, unasked. 'it might inspire people' is the most believable reason to advertise, and the poem still says let it go.

practice: Softly, out loud, name one view you praise a lot: about food, a team, music, people, anything. Then say, just as softly: that's my view.
Hear the difference between the view and the my, and breathe with that small gap until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Corrupted: the poem's name, for speech from a spoiled mind, and for the praising of your own view and virtue that leads straight into quarrels.

orig.note: Pali: view, opinion (Sanskrit dṛṣṭi). The chapter of eights keeps returning to it.

carryVoice: Carry this: my own view, worth holding gently and not worth advertising. That makes poem three.

sources.q: Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
